What makes the duck so amazing?

The duck that floats along on the water is an amazing waterbird — it paddles with webbed feet and has feathers that never get wet. And it's so adorable to watch a duckling waddle along right behind its mother!

We've gathered all kinds of stories about ducks — duck facts, duck webbed feet, and duck imprinting.

content.text:
Nature and science facts about the duck

The duck swims well by pushing against the water with the webbing between its toes. Its feathers are coated with oil so they don't get wet, so even when it comes out of the water it dries off quickly (it spreads the oil by preening its feathers with its beak). It filters water plants, bugs, and grains with its flat bill, and a newly hatched duckling has an imprinting habit — it treats the first moving thing it sees as its mother and follows it everywhere.

Parent guide — how to spark curiosity

Drop a bit of oil onto water to show how it "repels the water" (the feather principle). Watching a video of a duckling following its mother through imprinting makes it even more exciting.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. Why don't a duck's feathers get wet?
A. Because the feathers are coated with oil that repels water. The duck spreads the oil by preening its feathers with its beak.

Q. Why does a duckling waddle along behind its mother?
A. Because of "imprinting" — it treats the first moving thing it sees as its mother.

Q. How can we observe it at home?
A. Show the feather principle with a drop of oil on water, and watch an imprinting video.
